name: Iraq
headline: Iraq has no data protection law and mostly paper records; we found a legal right to a free record copy only in Kurdistan.

access.summary: Kurdistan's Law No. 4 of 2020 gives patients a free copy of their medical file, but we found no matching federal right for the rest of Iraq. The insurer's Damani platform holds an electronic file, but the patient features described are booking, covered services and remaining visits.
detail: Article 3 of the Kurdistan Region's Law No. 4 of 2020 gives every patient, in public or private care, the right to see their medical file and get a copy on request, and a medical report, without charge.

The Kurdistan health ministry's Instruction No. 4 of 2022 adds a right to request a medical report and copies of test results. It restates the right to see and copy the record in its section on patients with AIDS.
For federal Iraq we found no law giving patients a right to see or copy their record. A federal right was not verified, so the score stays in the band for rights that cover only some people.

The Health Insurance Fund says its Damani app lets members register, add family, see covered services and track how many yearly visits remain. Whether patients can open their own medical file in the app was not verified.

control.summary: In the state insurer's digital system, records are shared by default: a doctor who enters a Damani insurance number sees the patient's full medical history. We found no opt-out, consent choices or patient-visible access log.
detail: The Health Insurance Fund's director told the Iraqi News Agency in February 2026 that once a doctor enters the insurance number, the patient's whole medical history appears. No consent step or patient choice was described.
In April 2026 he said the system runs on biometric cards that serve as the insured person's medical file.

Kurdistan's 2022 instruction says information in the patient's file must be protected and kept confidential unless the patient or a court gives written authorisation. That limits disclosure to outsiders but gives no control over sharing inside the health system.
The Kurdistan law also bars showing a patient in media or social networks without their consent. We found no access log or opt-out anywhere in Iraq.

privacy.summary: Iraq has no data protection law and no data regulator, and a law firm notes there is no breach notification duty outside banking. Protection rests on the constitution's privacy clause and the Penal Code's secrecy offence.
detail: Article 17 of the 2005 Constitution gives every individual a right to personal privacy, as long as it does not contradict the rights of others and public morals.

Article 437 of the Penal Code punishes anyone who learns a secret through their job or profession and discloses it outside legal cases, with up to 2 years' detention. Article 438 punishes publishing information about another person's private or family life.
An August 2026 analysis by Muayad & Associates says Iraq has no data protection statute, no legal definition of sensitive data, no breach notification duty outside banking and no central regulator.

Kurdistan's patient law adds a duty to keep health information private, except where the law, a court or public health requires. Iraq has no EU adequacy decision, and the GDPR and the European Health Data Space do not apply.

commercial.summary: No law limits selling health data or using it for marketing, because Iraq has no data protection law. The only barrier we found is the Penal Code ban on professionals disclosing or profiting from secrets learned at work.
detail: Article 437 of the Penal Code covers anyone who discloses confidential information learned through their profession, or uses it for their own or another's advantage. That reaches doctors and staff, but says nothing about data brokers, apps or de-identified data.
Muayad & Associates wrote in August 2026 that, without a data protection law, Iraq has no legal definition of personal or sensitive data.

The Damani system was built with a private company under a partnership, at no cost to the state budget, the fund's director said. The data terms of that contract were not published in anything we opened.

journey.summary: Iraq's records are still mostly on paper. The state insurer's digital file covered about 2.7 million people in September 2026, mostly in Baghdad, and Kurdistan launched a unified hospital system in May 2026.
detail: A 2025 paper in Oxford Open Digital Health says Iraq's health information system is predominantly paper-based because past conflicts damaged infrastructure, and that the country lacks a nationwide electronic record.

The Health Insurance Authority says its digital system gives each member a medical file and an electronic card and links contracted providers. Coverage passed 2.7 million in Baghdad, with Najaf, Karbala and Basra joining and 6 more governorates planned.
In May 2026 the Kurdistan health ministry launched a system linking treatment, pharmacy, emergency, operating rooms and administration across the Region's hospitals.
For public health, WHO and the ministry began moving the immunisation programme onto DHIS2 in 2023, with other programmes to follow.

clinical.summary: Doctors at providers inside the health insurance scheme can pull up an insured patient's full history by insurance number. Outside that scheme, and outside new Kurdistan hospital systems, clinicians rely on paper files and reports the patient carries.
detail: The Health Insurance Fund says the electronic file ends the need for patients to keep paper reports and test results, and that the history appears as soon as the doctor enters the insurance number.

The scheme covers state employees and their families, social welfare recipients, people with disabilities and, by choice, retirees. Providers include private wings of public hospitals and private hospitals under the law.
Kurdistan's patient law requires the first doctor or facility to give the patient a full free report when they seek a second opinion. That is how records move between providers there.

research.summary: Kurdistan's patient law lets people join or refuse medical research and withdraw at any time, and the Penal Code punishes disclosing professional secrets. We found no rules on reusing health records, and national ethics review was not verified, so the score is 45.
detail: Article 3 of Kurdistan's Law No. 4 of 2020 lets a patient take part or not in any medical study or research, and withdraw whenever they wish.

A 2012 review of 13 Arab countries in BMC Medical Ethics found Iraq had no national research ethics guidelines. The ministry referred to guidelines from an unknown source. Whether national guidelines have been adopted since was not verified.
We found no law, register or opt-out covering reuse of health records or insurance data for research.

No consent and no opt-out cover reuse of records, so the anchors start at 40. Two safeguards count: the Kurdistan consent route and statutory secrecy under Penal Code Article 437, giving 46. The score is held to 45 because national ethics review was not verified.

ai.summary: Iraq has no AI law and no rules for AI in clinical care that we could find. A national AI strategy is still being drafted and is not binding.
detail: A June 2026 guide by Levellers says Iraq has no dedicated AI law and no data protection statute, and that the national AI strategy, coordinated from the Prime Minister's Office, is not enforceable law.

We found no medical device rules for AI software, no change control and no human oversight requirement. Reports of a health ministry committee drafting a health AI strategy in June 2026 were not verified on an official page.
Muayad & Associates notes Iraq has no binding cybersecurity or data protection statute, so no statute governs the data that health AI tools use.
